output.summary: Lacunar infarcts result from occlusion of a single deep perforating artery and present as a lacunar syndrome (pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis or dysarthria-clumsy hand). IV thrombolysis applies to disabling deficits within 4.5 hours whatever the stroke mechanism. Secondary prevention rests on single antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure control and lipid lowering.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not exclude acute ischemic stroke on the basis of a normal non-contrast CT alone — a normal CT is expected in acute lacunar stroke and does not rule out the diagnosis
Do not withhold consideration of IV tPA solely because the NIHSS is low (5) — if the deficit is functionally disabling (impaired grip, unable to ambulate safely), tPA eligibility must be assessed
Do not administer IV tPA before non-contrast CT excludes intracranial hemorrhage
Do not assume small-vessel mechanism without completing cardiac monitoring and vessel imaging to exclude competing etiologies
Do not give antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy within 24 hours of IV thrombolysis or before follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage.
Do not use long-term dual antiplatelet therapy for this lacunar stroke; in SPS3, clopidogrel added to aspirin increased bleeding and death without reducing recurrence.
required_recommendations: Establish last known well (09:45, witnessed onset, 33 minutes before arrival at 10:18) and the NIHSS (5).
Obtain non-contrast CT head FIRST to exclude intracranial hemorrhage before any thrombolytic decision
Recognize that a normal initial CT does not exclude acute lacunar stroke; MRI DWI may confirm the lacune after the reperfusion decision; do not delay IV thrombolysis for MRI.

IV thrombolysis: give (33 minutes from last known well; the pure motor deficit is disabling despite NIHSS 5, with a weak right grip (3/5) that made him drop a mug and a gait that needs assistance; no anticoagulant, INR 1.0, platelets 231, glucose 188 mg/dL, no haemorrhage on CT; blood pressure 172/96 mmHg is already below 185/110; daily aspirin is not a contraindication). Thrombectomy: not indicated because CTA shows no large vessel occlusion.
Achieve a door-to-needle time under 60 minutes.

Keep blood pressure below 185/110 mmHg until thrombolysis starts (172/96 mmHg on arrival needs no lowering now) and below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours afterwards, with IV labetalol or nicardipine if exceeded.
Monitor closely for orolingual angioedema during and after thrombolysis (he takes lisinopril, an ACE inhibitor).
Treat hyperglycaemia (glucose 188 mg/dL) to 140 to 180 mg/dL during the first 24 hours, avoiding hypoglycaemia with his glipizide.
Confirm sinus rhythm on ECG to support non-cardioembolic mechanism
Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac monitoring (telemetry) for at least the first 24 hours.
Classify mechanism as TOAST small-vessel occlusion after excluding large-vessel and cardioembolic sources

Start single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, or clopidogrel 75 mg daily) 24 hours after thrombolysis once follow-up imaging excludes haemorrhage; NIHSS 5 is above the threshold for 21-day dual antiplatelet therapy.
Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg daily (LDL 141 mg/dL on 40 mg, with diabetes and carotid plaque), check adherence, and recheck lipids in 4 to 12 weeks.

Set a long-term blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg: resume lisinopril and amlodipine once neurologically stable after the first 24 hours and intensify them (home readings have been high); optimise glycaemic control (HbA1c 8.4%) toward an individualised target near 7%.

key_clinical_evidence: The hallmark of a lacunar (small-vessel) stroke is a pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis, or dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome WITHOUT cortical signs — the absence of aphasia, neglect, gaze deviation, and visual field cut is diagnostically important and points away from a cortical MCA mechanism

Left internal capsule posterior limb lacune causes contralateral (right) pure motor face, arm, and leg weakness in equal proportion — the corticospinal tract is tightly bundled here, producing this classic equi-proportionate deficit

Acute lacunar infarcts are often invisible on non-contrast CT in the first hours; a normal CT does not exclude the diagnosis. DWI MRI confirms the small deep infarct, but it is obtained after the reperfusion decision and must not delay thrombolysis.
A modest NIHSS score may underestimate functional disability in lacunar stroke — an inability to grip or ambulate independently is disabling and qualifies for IV tPA consideration

Witnessed onset at 09:45 and arrival at 10:18 (33 minutes): within the 4.5-hour window. NIHSS 5 (facial palsy 1, right arm 2, right leg 2) with a disabling deficit (weak right grip, cannot walk safely without assistance), no anticoagulant, INR 1.0, platelets 231 and blood pressure 172/96 mmHg below 185/110: IV thrombolysis is indicated. CTA shows no large vessel occlusion, so thrombectomy does not apply.
TOAST small-vessel occlusion requires excluding both large-vessel disease (CTA) and a cardiac embolic source (ECG, echo, cardiac monitoring) before the lacunar mechanism is assigned

Secondary prevention of small-vessel stroke is driven by aggressive control of vascular risk factors — blood pressure is the most important modifiable risk factor, with a target SBP <130 mmHg; diabetes control (HbA1c) and high-intensity statin therapy are also critical

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Washington is a 62-year-old right-handed African American man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department after acute onset of right-sided weakness. He was in his usual state of health earlier this morning, watching television with his wife, when at approximately 09:45 he noted sudden-onset weakness of his right hand — he dropped his coffee mug when he tried to grip it. He immediately noticed that his right leg also felt heavy when he stood up, and his wife observed a subtle droop of the right side of his face. She called 911 without delay. EMS arrived at 09:57 and documented right facial droop, right arm and leg weakness, and a Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale score of 2. The patient's speech was noted to be entirely normal by EMS personnel. Fingerstick glucose in the field was 168 mg/dL. He was transported emergently and arrived in the emergency department at 10:18, approximately 33 minutes after symptom onset. The patient denies any headache, nausea, vomiting, vision changes, double vision, slurred speech, dizziness, loss of consciousness, or prior similar episodes. He reports no sensation of numbness or tingling in any limb — the deficit is purely weakness. He is able to speak clearly and is not confused. His wife confirms he was entirely at his baseline until the weakness began at 09:45. He has no history of prior stroke, TIA, seizure, or cardiac arrhythmia. He takes his antihypertensive and diabetic medications regularly but acknowledges his blood pressure has been elevated on home monitoring for the past several weeks. He denies any recent surgery or trauma and takes no anticoagulant; his only antithrombotic is daily aspirin.
